680514.long_answer: Rapp-Hodgkin syndrome is an autosomal-dominant ectodermal dysplasia caused by TP63 mutations. Its clinical picture includes limb malformations such as partial syndactyly together with sparse, coarse scalp hair. Microscopic examination of the hair shaft shows marked (‘exaggerated’) pili torti, making this syndrome the recognized condition that combines syndactyly with pronounced pili torti.

977469.long_answer: Severe and lethal osteogenesis imperfecta (types II and III) most often result from missense point mutations in the COL1A1 or COL1A2 genes that replace the obligatory glycine residues in the Gly-X-Y repeats of type I collagen. These glycine-substitution mutations disrupt the triple-helix structure, producing structurally abnormal collagen that exerts a dominant-negative effect, leading to the severe clinical phenotypes.

454775.long_answer: Cerebellar degeneration often impairs coordination of the oropharyngeal muscles, producing dysphagia (difficulty swallowing). When swallowing is ineffective, food or liquids can enter the airway, predisposing patients to aspiration pneumonia if the dysphagia is not managed.

946729.long_answer: Pathogenic loss-of-function mutations in SCNN1B, the gene that encodes the β-subunit of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), cause the systemic form of Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1. ENaC is also expressed in the uterine and endometrial epithelium, where its sodium-transport activity is crucial for fluid absorption and embryo implantation. Consequently, women with SCNN1B mutations can have defective endometrial receptivity and experience primary infertility in addition to the salt-wasting features of PHA-1.

135112.long_answer: Although Adams–Oliver syndrome is usually inherited as a germ-line autosomal-dominant or autosomal-recessive trait, several documented patients (and some transmitting parents) carry the pathogenic variant only in a subset of their cells. This somatic or gonadal mosaicism is a recognized but rare genetic phenomenon associated with Adams–Oliver syndrome and explains otherwise sporadic or variably expressed cases.

951619.long_answer: When a pleural effusion arises as a direct consequence of medical or surgical intervention—such as thoracic surgery, central line placement, or drug therapy—the cause is termed 'iatrogenic.' The adjective denotes any condition induced unintentionally by diagnostic or therapeutic procedures performed by healthcare professionals.

295056.long_answer: The MYO7A gene, which encodes the motor protein myosin VIIA and whose mutations cause Usher syndrome type I (specifically the USH1B subtype) as well as some forms of non-syndromic deafness, is located on chromosome 11 (cytogenetic band 11q13.5). It is not situated on chromosome 16. Therefore, the statement that MYO7A is found on chromosome 16 is incorrect.

779077.long_answer: In media profiles of one of the oldest known survivors of the extremely rare over-growth disorder MOMO syndrome, the teenager states that his goal for the future is to go to college. This aspiration—pursuing higher education—has been repeatedly highlighted as a milestone he hopes to achieve despite the medical challenges associated with the syndrome.

371752.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the X-linked gene FLNA (filamin A) are a recognised cause of chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction.  Filamin A is an actin-binding cytoskeletal protein that interacts with guidance receptors such as ROBO and netrin receptors, helping to steer axon growth cones.  Through these interactions FLNA is required for proper motor-neuron outgrowth and positioning during embryonic development, placing the gene in the Gene Ontology category “motor neuron development.”

621373.long_answer: Split hand split foot-nystagmus syndrome is characterized mainly by ectrodactyly (split hand/foot malformation). Corrective surgery, prosthetic fitting, and long-term functional care for these complex limb anomalies are undertaken by orthopedic surgeons, usually hand- and foot-specialized orthopedists. While ophthalmology may address the associated nystagmus, the core therapeutic management of the syndrome’s hallmark skeletal defects lies within the orthopedic specialty.

474236.long_answer: Chronic mountain sickness (Monge’s disease) results from prolonged hypobaric hypoxia at high altitude, leading to ventilatory impairment, severe polycythemia, pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart strain. Management focuses on improving oxygenation (descent, supplemental O₂, acetazolamide) and controlling related pulmonary complications, all of which fall under the expertise of pulmonology/respiratory medicine specialists.

974805.long_answer: Trisomy 9 is a chromosomal aneuploidy; its confirmation requires cytogenetic testing and its care plan involves evaluation of multisystem anomalies and genetic counseling. These activities fall within the purview of the medical genetics specialty, which is responsible for diagnosing chromosomal disorders and guiding their clinical management.

794379.long_answer: The gravest complication of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is cardiac involvement, most notably necrotising vasculitis of the coronary arteries. Coronary arteritis can lead to myocarditis, heart failure, and fatal arrhythmias, making these arteries the critical vessels affected in the disease’s most serious manifestation.

868957.long_answer: Aplasia is the medical term for the complete failure of an organ or tissue to develop during embryogenesis. In disorders such as Larsen syndrome, various structures—including bones, ligaments, or other organs—may be absent because they are aplastic, meaning they never formed in the first place.

386890.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the X-linked ZIC3 gene are a recognized cause of heterotaxy with atrial isomerism. Because the trait is X-linked, a carrier mother has a 50 % chance of passing the mutation to each pregnancy; affected male fetuses frequently develop atrial isomerism and complex congenital heart disease. Identifying a ZIC3 mutation therefore provides critical information for genetic counselling, recurrence-risk assessment, and targeted prenatal or pre-implantation testing in the family.

316300.long_answer: In recurrent respiratory (laryngeal) papillomatosis, repeated endoscopic debulking or laser excisions are the standard treatment. When papillomas recur so rapidly that airway obstruction persists despite multiple debulkings, a tracheostomy can be performed to bypass the obstructed laryngeal airway and secure long-term ventilation. Although tracheostomy is avoided when possible because it may facilitate distal spread of papillomas, it remains the definitive surgical option for severe, refractory cases where other surgical and adjuvant measures have failed.

306612.long_answer: Clinical surveys of 48,XXYY males show a high rate of recurrent or chronic otitis media (middle-ear infections). Craniofacial differences and eustachian-tube dysfunction in this aneuploidy increase the likelihood of fluid retention and infection in the middle ear, making otitis media a common ear problem in individuals with XXYY syndrome.

176377.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the LYST (lysosomal trafficking regulator) gene are the classical cause of Chédiak–Higashi syndrome.  Because LYST is essential for proper maturation and transport of melanosomes in melanocytes, certain LYST mutations also give rise to pigmentary abnormalities and sensorineural deafness that meet clinical criteria for Waardenburg syndrome type 2.  Thus, mutation of the single gene LYST underlies both Chédiak–Higashi syndrome and Waardenburg syndrome type 2.

693015.long_answer: In Meige’s syndrome, dystonic activity frequently involves the muscles that move the mandible. Bilateral involuntary contraction of the lateral pterygoid muscles pulls the mandible anteriorly, producing protrusion of the jaw so that the chin is thrust forward.

456441.long_answer: Drugs with anticholinergic activity (such as many antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, antispasmodics) block muscarinic parasympathetic stimulation of the salivary glands, markedly reducing saliva flow (xerostomia). The resulting salivary stasis predisposes the parotid or submandibular glands to ascending bacterial infection and inflammation, producing sialadenitis.

143083.long_answer: In Canavan’s disease, N-acetylaspartate (NAA) is made inside neuronal mitochondria. Because aspartoacylase is deficient, the NAA that is synthesized in mitochondria cannot be degraded in oligodendrocytes, so it accumulates excessively and the brain is deprived of the acetate needed for myelin lipid production. Thus, mitochondrial production of NAA is the upstream metabolic step that drives the pathological build-up of NAA and contributes to the dysmyelination characteristic of the disease.

847237.long_answer: Mutations in the KRIT1 gene, also called CCM1, are a well-established cause of familial cerebral cavernous hemangiomas. Experimental deletion of Krit1 in mice disrupts endothelial-cell junctions and vascular morphogenesis, leading to severe hemorrhage and death during mid-gestation, demonstrating that loss of this gene is embryonically lethal in mice.

417624.long_answer: Pipecolic acidemia is an inborn error of metabolism caused by a hereditary defect in peroxisomal pipecolic acid oxidation. Disorders of this type are evaluated through specialized metabolic testing and molecular genetic analysis, and their ongoing management (including genetic counseling, dietary or enzyme-based therapies, and monitoring for neurological sequelae) is overseen by physicians trained in medical genetics/biochemical genetics. Therefore, the medical genetics specialty is the one that typically diagnoses and treats pipecolic acidemia.

644830.long_answer: In the families described with Corneal-cerebellar syndrome, the disorder appears only when both copies of the causal gene are mutated, while clinically normal parents transmit the mutation to affected offspring. This carrier-parent/affected-child pattern is the hallmark of autosomal-recessive inheritance, which is the accepted mode of transmission for Corneal-cerebellar syndrome.

219753.long_answer: Misoprostol, a synthetic prostaglandin E1 analogue, is sometimes used topically (e.g., as a mouth-rinse or tablet applied to the lesion) to promote healing and pain relief in recurrent aphthous stomatitis. Systemically, the same drug is well established in obstetrics for cervical ripening and stimulation of uterine contractions, making it a standard agent for induction of labor and medical termination of pregnancy. Thus, misoprostol links the two clinical uses referenced in the question.

620103.long_answer: The syndrome known as Trigonocephaly-bifid nose-acral anomalies (also called acromelic frontonasal dysostosis) has been shown to result from heterozygous missense mutations in the ZSWIM6 gene. Pathogenic variants such as p.Arg1295Leu in ZSWIM6 disrupt embryonic craniofacial and limb development, producing the characteristic combination of metopic craniosynostosis (trigonocephaly), bifid or broad nasal tip, and distal limb (acral) anomalies.

104913.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in RBPJ (Recombination Signal Binding Protein for Immunoglobulin κ J region) cause Adams–Oliver syndrome type 2. Independent genome-wide association and candidate-gene studies have also identified common and rare RBPJ variants as risk factors for nonsyndromic cleft lip with or without cleft palate, linking this Notch-pathway transcription factor to both conditions.

578362.long_answer: NARP syndrome (Neuropathy, Ataxia, and Retinitis Pigmentosa) primarily affects the nervous system—peripheral nerves, cerebellar pathways, and sometimes the visual pathways—making its diagnosis and management the domain of a neurologist, the specialist trained to evaluate, diagnose, and treat neurological disorders.

546714.long_answer: The term for an excessive, irrational fear of odors is olfactophobia. It combines the Latin stem "olfacto-" (from olfacere, “to smell”) with the Greek suffix "-phobia" (fear). Clinically, people with olfactophobia experience marked anxiety or avoidance behaviors when exposed to certain smells, distinguishing it from the more commonly cited Greek-derived term “osmophobia.”

700408.long_answer: The median (midline) cleft of the mandible and lower lip (Tessier no. 30) is a rare congenital malformation produced by failure of fusion of the paired mandibular prominences. Because this fusion defect leaves part of the tongue tethered to the floor of the mouth, an abnormally short or persistent frenulum linguae (ankyloglossia) is almost always present. Thus the malformation simultaneously involves a midline facial cleft and an abnormal frenulum linguae.

874734.long_answer: Non-polio enteroviruses, particularly Coxsackie A and B viruses, are well-documented causes of acute viral gastroenteritis in children. The same enteroviruses have repeatedly been identified as precipitating infections in patients who later develop myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), with studies showing elevated enteroviral RNA or antibodies in ME/CFS cohorts. Thus, enterovirus infection is a recognized common trigger for both pediatric gastroenteritis and the onset of ME/CFS.

891507.long_answer: The FUS (fused in sarcoma) gene, mapped to chromosome 16p11.2, encodes an RNA-binding protein. Pathogenic FUS mutations are a well-established cause of autosomal dominant frontotemporal dementia that can present with parkinsonism, linking this chromosome-16 gene to the disorder.

641187.long_answer: Heterozygous pathogenic variants in the NKX2-5 homeobox transcription factor gene are a well-established cause of familial secundum atrial septal defects. NKX2-5 directs cardiac septation during embryogenesis, and loss-of-function mutations disrupt this process, leading to ASDs (often with atrioventricular conduction block). These variants are routinely detectable by clinical cardiac gene panels or exome sequencing, making NKX2-5 mutation the canonical genetic defect identified through testing in patients with atrial septal defects.

140495.long_answer: Clindamycin is a lincosamide antibiotic routinely prescribed for bacterial infections. Topical clindamycin has also been reported to lessen the pruritic papules of Fox-Fordyce disease by reducing inflammation and bacterial colonization in the affected apocrine follicles.

157580.long_answer: Mutations in the CLN3 gene (responsible for the classic juvenile form of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, or Batten disease) not only produce progressive neurodegeneration but also lead to lysosomal storage within cardiomyocytes, causing hypertrophic changes, conduction abnormalities, and other myocardial pathology. Thus, the CLN3 gene mutation is the NCL-associated defect known to affect the myocardium.

297502.long_answer: In the International Classification of Diseases, Asperger syndrome remained a distinct diagnosis through ICD-10. It was subsumed under the single category “autism spectrum disorder” in the next revision, ICD-11, which officially came into effect on 1 January 2022; from that date the separate Asperger syndrome code ceased to exist.

654698.long_answer: Gliomas of the second cranial (optic) nerve are generally low-grade tumors that rarely threaten life, but they can rapidly impair visual function. Therefore, therapeutic decisions (observation, chemotherapy, limited surgery or radiotherapy) are guided mainly by eyesight considerations. The overarching, widely accepted goal is to maintain or maximize the patient’s remaining visual acuity rather than to achieve total tumor eradication.

684608.long_answer: Legionella pneumophila survives and multiplies inside alveolar macrophages. Aminoglycoside antibiotics do not enter eukaryotic cells efficiently, so therapeutic concentrations are not achieved within these infected macrophages. Because of this poor intracellular penetration, aminoglycosides cannot reliably reach or kill the intracellular Legionella organisms, making them ineffective and therefore not recommended for treating Legionnaires' disease.

633112.long_answer: AIDS selectively destroys CD4⁺ T-helper cells, crippling cell-mediated immunity. Because Type IV (delayed-type, T-cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reactions require intact CD4⁺ Th1 cells to activate macrophages and cytotoxic T lymphocytes, this class of hypersensitivity is markedly impaired in patients with AIDS.

122286.long_answer: Multiple sulfatase deficiency results from loss of activity of all lysosomal sulfatase enzymes. Without these enzymes, sulfate groups cannot be removed from their substrates, so the sulfated sphingolipid sulfatides and the sulfated polysaccharides (glycosaminoglycans such as heparan and dermatan sulfate) are not degraded and progressively build up inside lysosomes, producing the characteristic lysosomal storage pathology of the disease.

829736.long_answer: Epidemiological and metabolic studies show that inadequate vitamin C (ascorbic acid) intake raises gallstone risk. Vitamin C is a required co-factor for cholesterol 7-α-hydroxylase, the enzyme that converts cholesterol into bile acids. When vitamin C is lacking, bile acid synthesis falls, bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol, and cholesterol precipitates to form gallstones. Populations with low plasma vitamin C or dietary intake consistently exhibit a higher prevalence of cholesterol gallstones.

388426.long_answer: During complicated delivery or septic/unsafe abortion, large amounts of tissue factor enter the maternal circulation, triggering disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). The widespread activation of the coagulation cascade causes micro-vascular thrombosis, leading to ischemia and tissue necrosis while simultaneously consuming clotting factors and platelets.

996805.long_answer: In osteogenesis imperfecta the bones are extremely fragile; the weight and leverage of a hip spica cast can place excessive stress on adjacent brittle bones, often causing new (iatrogenic) fractures during application or while the cast is in place. To avoid provoking additional fractures, lighter immobilization or internal fixation is preferred over a hip spica cast in these patients.

821875.long_answer: Phosphoglucomutase-1 (PGM1) was originally labelled as the cause of glycogen storage disease type XIV, because loss of its activity disturbs the interconversion of glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate and leads to abnormal glycogen handling. Subsequent work showed that the same block critically limits formation of UDP-glucose and UDP-galactose, precursors needed to build N-linked glycans. Because the dominant clinical mechanism proved to be a defect in protein N-glycosylation, the condition was re-classified as PGM1-CDG (a congenital disorder of glycosylation) and the gene PGM1 was de-listed as a classical glycogen storage disease gene.

423233.long_answer: Unverricht–Lundborg disease (progressive myoclonus epilepsy type 1) is driven by an unstable polymeric array of a 12-base-pair minisatellite (dodecamer) in the promoter of the CSTB (cystatin B) gene. Pathogenic expansion of this dodecamer repeat reduces CSTB expression, and the size of the repeat polymer correlates with disease onset and severity, making the dodecamer repeat expansion the key polymeric structure in disease progression.

483573.long_answer: Treponema pallidum, the spirochete responsible for human syphilis, is a species in the genus Treponema. This genus is classified within the family Spirochaetaceae, one of the four recognized families in the order Spirochaetales. Therefore, the family that includes the syphilis pathogen is Spirochaetaceae.

447656.long_answer: In Glycogen storage disease type VI (Hers disease), defective hepatic glycogen phosphorylase limits glucose release during fasting. The body compensates with increased lipolysis and ketogenesis, which can chronically elevate plasma triglycerides and cholesterol. This persistent hyperlipidemia is a recognized complication of GSD VI and often necessitates ongoing lipid-lowering medication to keep blood lipid levels within a safe range.

419678.long_answer: Carbamazepine, an anticonvulsant that enhances the release and action of endogenous vasopressin, can reduce polyuria and polydipsia in patients with central diabetes insipidus and is therefore sometimes used as adjunct or alternative therapy when desmopressin is not suitable.

701870.long_answer: In classical descriptions of smallpox, the febrile prodrome is normally followed by the characteristic vesicular-pustular skin eruption. Rarely, infection produces only the prodromal fever and toxemia without any cutaneous lesions; such rash-less cases were historically termed “variola sine eruptione,” literally ‘smallpox without eruption.’

212018.long_answer: Foix–Chavany–Marie (opercular) syndrome is confirmed not only with neuro-imaging but also by detailed language evaluation; clinicians perform psycholinguistic testing, which examines how linguistic abilities relate to underlying cognitive and psychological processes. This form of assessment distinguishes the voluntary speech impairment typical of the syndrome from primary aphasic disorders.

739090.long_answer: The characteristic cytogenetic abnormality of follicular lymphoma is the t(14;18)(q32;q21) translocation, which juxtaposes the BCL2 gene on chromosome 18 to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus on chromosome 14, leading to over-expression of BCL2 and inhibition of apoptosis. A t(16;18) translocation is not part of the established cytogenetic profile of follicular lymphoma and is not regarded as a defining or common alteration for this disease. Therefore, follicular lymphoma is not linked to t(16;18).

166248.long_answer: Severe alcoholism is frequently accompanied by malnutrition, particularly a deficiency of vitamin C. Without adequate vitamin C, proline and lysine in collagen cannot be hydroxylated, preventing proper cross-linking of collagen fibers. The resulting weak connective tissue in the aortic media and adventitia cannot resist intraluminal pressure, so the aortic wall dilates and is more prone to form an aneurysm. Thus, alcoholism raises aortic aneurysm risk mainly through vitamin C–deficiency-mediated weakening of the vessel wall.

615664.long_answer: Genome-wide association studies have repeatedly linked the SH2B3 gene, which encodes the adaptor protein LNK, to multiple complex traits. The nonsynonymous variant rs3184504 (R262W) in SH2B3 shows strong association with elevated systolic and diastolic blood pressure and therefore essential hypertension. The same variant is also one of the most replicated risk loci for autoimmune diseases, including type 1 diabetes, where altered SH2B3 signaling affects lymphocyte activation and tolerance. Thus, SH2B3 is a single gene convincingly associated with both essential hypertension and type 1 diabetes.

298712.long_answer: Germ-line loss-of-function mutations in the PTCH1 gene, which encodes the Patched-1 receptor in the Hedgehog signalling pathway, cause basal cell naevus (Gorlin–Goltz) syndrome. A hallmark of this syndrome is the development of multiple basal-cell carcinomas, and affected patients also characteristically form excessive wound-healing responses, leading to hypertrophic or keloid-type scars after even minor trauma or surgery. Thus the same PTCH1 mutation is linked to both basal-cell carcinoma and hypertrophic scarring.

244121.long_answer: Kozlowski-Krajewska syndrome is another name for the Kozlowski type of spondylometaphyseal dysplasia—a hereditary skeletal dysplasia that causes abnormal development of the spine, long-bone metaphyses and epiphyses, short stature, coxa vara and other bone deformities. Management centers on monitoring growth, correcting limb and spinal deformities, and, when necessary, performing surgical procedures such as osteotomies or spinal fusion. These evaluations and interventions are carried out primarily by orthopedic surgeons (often pediatric orthopedists), making orthopedics the specialty most likely to handle treatment.

153682.long_answer: Children with Cockayne syndrome often show pituitary growth-hormone (GH) deficiency, which contributes to their severe post-natal growth failure. Published case reports document catch-up growth when affected children were given recombinant human growth hormone. GH restores circulating IGF-1 and stimulates longitudinal bone growth, making it the hormone considered for therapeutic use in this setting.

732214.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in ABCC8, which encodes the SUR1 subunit of the pancreatic β-cell KATP channel, can produce opposite functional effects. Activating mutations reduce insulin secretion and lead to transient neonatal diabetes mellitus, whereas inactivating (loss-of-function) mutations cause excessive insulin release and congenital hyperinsulinism. Thus the same gene, ABCC8, is well-established to underlie both conditions.

305633.long_answer: During steel manufacture, ferromanganese alloys are added and workers are chronically exposed to manganese-containing dusts and fumes. Inhalation of these aerosols can produce systemic manganese toxicity (“manganism”), an occupational disease characterized by neuro-behavioural and Parkinson-like features. Hence, manganese poisoning is the classic occupational disease linked to the iron and steel industry.

682355.long_answer: The first officially recognized Minamata-disease patient—a 5-year-old girl admitted on 21 April 1956—died from severe neurological damage produced by methylmercury poisoning. Industrial effluent from the Chisso chemical plant had contaminated fish and shellfish in Minamata Bay with methylmercury; ingestion of this neurotoxin led to irreversible central-nervous-system degeneration, respiratory failure, and ultimately death in the index case.

513730.long_answer: In amyoplasia-type arthrogryposis the wrist characteristically sits in flexion with marked ulnar deviation. This mal-alignment is produced by bowing and relative overgrowth of the distal ulna; corrective operations frequently include distal-ulnar shortening or wedge osteotomy. Thus, the bone primarily involved in the typical wrist deformity is the distal ulna.

422015.long_answer: A naturally occurring form of glycogen storage disease type V has been documented in Charolais cattle. A recessive mutation in the PYGM gene abolishes muscle glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase) activity, so affected Charolais animals lack this enzyme in skeletal muscle, providing the classic example of myophosphorylase deficiency in cattle.

451691.long_answer: Biologic agents that block tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α)—such as infliximab, etanercept and adalimumab—are established treatments for psoriatic arthritis. Because SAPHO syndrome shares a TNF-α-driven inflammatory mechanism, several case reports and small series have shown clinical and radiological improvement when patients with SAPHO were treated with these TNF-α inhibitors, so this drug class is often recommended when first-line therapies fail.

272631.long_answer: First-line therapy for many neuroendocrine tumors involves long-acting somatostatin analogs (e.g., octreotide LAR), which are routinely delivered as depot intramuscular injections every 4 weeks. This injection route provides sustained drug release, controls hormone-related symptoms, and slows tumor growth, making intramuscular administration a common treatment method in NET patients.

577043.long_answer: Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome—a congenital long-QT syndrome associated with sensorineural deafness—was first documented in 1957 by Anton Jervell and Fred Lange-Nielsen in Oslo, Norway, where they described a Norwegian family exhibiting prolonged QT intervals, syncopal episodes, and congenital deaf-mutism.

301821.long_answer: Repeated mechanical and inflammatory irritation of the intestinal mucosa by retained enteroliths in diverticula has been reported to promote malignant transformation of the epithelial lining, with several case reports describing the development of adenocarcinoma arising within those chronically inflamed diverticula.

285469.long_answer: In laboratory and wild populations, Mus musculus typically survives for roughly two years on average, with the oldest individuals rarely exceeding three years; mice beyond 18–24 months are therefore considered elderly.

146625.long_answer: Melanoma risk is increased by germ-line mutations in the XPC gene. XPC encodes the DNA-damage-recognition factor of nucleotide-excision repair; when it is mutated, cells cannot efficiently repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers, leading to accumulation of mutations and a strong predisposition to skin cancers such as melanoma.

347482.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the MYO1A gene, located on human chromosome 12q12-q14, cause autosomal-dominant nonsyndromic sensorineural deafness (designated DFNA48). MYO1A encodes the unconventional motor protein myosin IA, which is essential for proper organization and tension of actin-rich stereocilia in the cochlear hair cells; disruption of this protein impairs mechano-electrical transduction and leads to isolated hearing loss without additional syndromic features.

158772.long_answer: Polymorphisms in the MYH9 (non-muscle myosin heavy-chain 9) locus on chromosome 22 are a well-established genetic risk factor for a wide range of nondiabetic end-stage renal diseases—such as focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, HIV-associated nephropathy, and hypertension-attributed ESRD. In addition, pathogenic MYH9 mutations can produce glomerular involvement and platelet abnormalities that lead to microscopic or gross hematuria, linking this same locus to episodes of blood in the urine.

146290.long_answer: Individuals with adenosine monophosphate deaminase deficiency type 1 already have impaired muscle energy metabolism; adding a statin further stresses skeletal‐muscle cells and markedly raises the danger of statin-induced myopathy progressing to rhabdomyolysis—acute, widespread muscle breakdown that can lead to kidney injury.

981979.long_answer: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is a congenital overgrowth disorder caused by altered imprinting of genes on chromosome 11p15. Clinical hallmarks such as prenatal and birth macrosomia, macroglossia and abdominal wall defects are evident in the newborn period, so the condition is usually detectable at birth. The syndrome is extensively documented in public-domain sources such as MedlinePlus, GARD and open-access literature.

835593.long_answer: The optic nerve is composed of retinal ganglion-cell axons, which are part of the central nervous system (CNS). Unlike peripheral nerves, mature CNS axons lack the intrinsic growth programs and supportive glial environment needed for regrowth. After injury, oligodendrocyte-derived inhibitors (e.g., Nogo-A, MAG) and the glial scar prevent axonal extension, and the neurons themselves do not re-enter a regenerative state. Because these axons cannot reconnect to their targets in the brain, visual signals cannot be transmitted, making optic-nerve damage essentially permanent and blindness irreversible.

120869.long_answer: Females with trisomy X (47,XXX) often exhibit a fine or intention tremor as part of their mild neurological and motor‐coordination difficulties. Tremor is likewise a cardinal motor manifestation of several neurological disorders, most famously Parkinson’s disease, where loss of dopaminergic neurons produces resting tremor. Thus, tremor is a symptom common to both trisomy X and neurological diseases such as Parkinson’s.

139165.long_answer: Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita (SEDc) is an inherited skeletal dysplasia caused by pathogenic variants in the COL2A1 gene encoding type II collagen. Defective collagen disrupts endochondral ossification, producing markedly flattened vertebral bodies (platyspondyly) throughout the spine and early-onset thoracic scoliosis/kyphosis. These characteristic spinal changes, often noted on neonatal radiographs, distinguish SEDc from other causes of spinal deformity.

140808.long_answer: Mutations in the KRT1 gene, which encodes keratin 1, have been documented to cause both epidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma (Vörner type, showing epidermolytic hyperkeratosis) and nonepidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma (Unna-Thost type, lacking epidermolysis). Thus keratin 1 is uniquely linked to both histologic variants of palmoplantar keratoderma.

776486.long_answer: In symptomatic tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica, nodular bony/cartilaginous outgrowths can narrow the tracheobronchial lumen.  Endobronchial debulking with a neodymium-doped yttrium-aluminium-garnet (Nd:YAG) laser performed through a rigid or flexible bronchoscope is the standard therapeutic procedure to vaporise or core out the obstructing nodules and promptly restore airway patency.

834734.long_answer: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) has been linked to chronic nasal carriage of Staphylococcus aureus, which is thought to provide a persistent antigenic stimulus that may trigger or exacerbate the auto-immune response leading to ANCA production. Staphylococcus aureus is also a well-recognized, common bacterial cause of community- and hospital-acquired pneumonia, making it the pathogen that fulfills both aspects of the question.

377356.long_answer: Acute interstitial pneumonitis (Hamman–Rich syndrome) progresses rapidly to severe hypoxemic respiratory failure. No drug therapy has proven benefit; survival depends on aggressive supportive care. Endotracheal intubation with mechanical ventilation—usually delivered and monitored in an intensive care unit—is therefore regarded as the only consistently successful treatment.

384027.long_answer: Larsen syndrome can be accompanied by progressive dilation of the ascending aorta/aortic root, similar to that seen in other connective-tissue disorders. To slow aortic root enlargement and reduce wall stress, beta-blockade with propranolol is recommended, mirroring the strategy used in Marfan syndrome and related conditions.

776128.long_answer: Platelets with normal dense granules actively take up the fluorescent antibiotic mepacrine (also called quinacrine). In δ-storage pool deficiency the dense granules are absent or reduced, so platelets fail to accumulate mepacrine, providing a simple diagnostic test for this form of platelet storage pool deficiency.

842561.long_answer: In hereditary spherocytosis mutations in membrane-skeleton proteins (e.g., spectrin, ankyrin) cause loss of plasma-membrane fragments, so red cells become spherical instead of biconcave. The spherical shape has a smaller surface area relative to its volume, providing fewer membrane sites for diffusion of O₂ and CO₂. This reduced surface area-to-volume ratio limits the efficiency of gas exchange across the red-blood-cell membrane.

337186.long_answer: ARHGAP31, which encodes a Rho-GTPase–activating protein, is a well-established autosomal-dominant cause of Adams–Oliver syndrome. In the reported testing, sequencing of ARHGAP31 was performed but no pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were detected, indicating that this particular case of Adams–Oliver syndrome was not due to mutations in ARHGAP31.

597638.long_answer: Banti’s syndrome (non-cirrhotic portal hypertension with congestive splenomegaly) shows a chronic productive, or proliferative, inflammation of the portal and splenic veins—an obliterative phlebitis in which fibrous tissue gradually replaces the vessel wall. This chronic productive inflammatory process underlies the vascular obstruction that characterises the syndrome.

833592.long_answer: Cat-eye syndrome (Schmid-Fraccaro syndrome) is produced by partial trisomy/tetrasomy of the 22q11.2 segment. Within this duplicated segment, the dosage-sensitive gene CECR2 (Cat Eye Syndrome Chromosome Region, candidate 2) has been identified as a major contributor to the characteristic ocular coloboma and other developmental anomalies seen in the disorder.

552406.long_answer: People with schizotypal personality disorder often hold a rigid, hunched or self-protective posture—arms crossed, limited gesturing, little eye contact. This closed body language non-verbally signals anxiety and social withdrawal, so observers interpret them as aloof or odd and tend to keep their distance. Consequently, the posture reduces opportunities for positive social engagement and reinforces the individual’s social isolation.

673173.long_answer: An intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) can be inserted percutaneously to provide temporary circulatory support in acute decompensated heart failure secondary to severe aortic stenosis. The IABP inflates during diastole to augment coronary perfusion and deflates just before systole to reduce left-ventricular afterload, thereby stabilizing hemodynamics until definitive aortic valve intervention can be performed.

620580.long_answer: In viral croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) the parainfluenza virus triggers a predominantly lymphocytic inflammatory response. These lymphocytes infiltrate the mucosa and submucosa of the larynx and trachea, leading to edema and the characteristic airway swelling and narrowing that produce the stridor and barking cough of croup.

187939.long_answer: The term “encopresis” is derived from the Greek words “en” (in) and “kopros” (feces or dung), literally meaning ‘in feces.’ It was coined to describe the condition in which toilet-trained children aged four years or older involuntarily pass stool in inappropriate places.

138198.long_answer: During the 2017 Marburg virus outbreak in eastern Uganda, a 38-year-old male health-care worker who had treated earlier patients began feeling ill on 5 November 2017 while in Kapchorwa town (Kapchorwa District). Laboratory testing later confirmed that his illness was Marburg virus disease.

667323.long_answer: Heterozygous loss- or gain-of-function mutations in the transcription factor gene MAF (v-maf musculoaponeurotic fibrosarcoma oncogene homolog) have been recurrently reported in families that present with the classic Cataract-microcornea syndrome. The same MAF mutations are also documented in patients who, in addition to cataract and microcornea, show peripheral sclerocornea, indicating that alteration of MAF is the genetic lesion common to both phenotypes.

279699.long_answer: Tramadol is an atypical opioid analgesic frequently prescribed for peripheral (neuropathic) pain. It acts as a µ-opioid receptor agonist and inhibits reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine. The opioid component can produce dose-dependent respiratory depression, while the serotonergic activity can precipitate serotonin syndrome, especially when combined with other serotonergic drugs. These dual mechanisms explain why tramadol both treats neuropathic pain and carries risks of respiratory depression and serotonin syndrome.

781651.long_answer: A small latent outward deviation of the eyes (exophoria) is frequently observed in childhood; most school-aged children exhibit a mild exophoria that they control with strong fusional convergence reserves, making this age group the one in which exophoria is particularly common.

156307.long_answer: In Coats’ disease the yellow-white subretinal exudate is rich in lipid material, and microscopic examination shows numerous cholesterol crystals. Cholesterol is likewise liberated during degradation of red blood cells—the membrane lipids released as hemoglobin is broken down are converted to free cholesterol that can precipitate as crystals. Hence cholesterol is the common substance found both in Coats’ subretinal exudate and as a by-product of hemoglobin breakdown.

679391.long_answer: In diffuse panbronchiolitis, inflammation and mucus accumulation in the small airways produce discontinuous, popping sounds during inspiration. These bilateral coarse crackles (rales) are readily heard on chest auscultation with a stethoscope and are a characteristic physical finding of the disease.

693659.long_answer: Children born with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita are routinely started on intensive physical therapy to stretch contracted joints, improve range of motion, and strengthen muscles. Early, ongoing physiotherapy is the cornerstone of non-surgical management and is recommended by standard clinical guidelines for this condition.

773960.long_answer: A laryngocele is an air-filled dilation of the laryngeal saccule that enlarges when intralaryngeal pressure is repeatedly raised. People who blow glass for a living generate sustained high expiratory pressures, and the condition has historically been nicknamed “glass-blower’s disease.” Therefore, the occupation classically linked to an increased risk of laryngocele is glassblowing.

295666.long_answer: Foix–Alajouanine syndrome is a progressive myelopathy produced by a spinal arteriovenous malformation. Patients are typically evaluated and the vascular lesion is identified by a neurologist, who directs spinal MRI and catheter angiography to establish the diagnosis; therefore, neurology is the medical specialty responsible for diagnosing the causative arteriovenous malformation.

107800.long_answer: Dominant mutations in the SOS1 gene—an activator of RAS—have been identified in families showing gingival fibromatosis accompanied by hypertrichosis. SOS1 lies upstream of RAF, MEK and ERK, so these mutations hyper-activate the RAS–MAPK signalling cascade. Hence the disorder is classified as a RASopathy, directly implicating the RAS-MAPK pathway.

352046.long_answer: Loss-of-function (absence) of the coenzyme-Q2 polyprenyltransferase gene COQ2, especially the East-Asian V393A variant and other null mutations, leads to reduced CoQ10 biosynthesis and has been shown (Science 2013) to occur far more frequently in Japanese and other Asian patients with multiple system atrophy than in controls, linking absence of functional COQ2 to the disease in these populations.

193994.long_answer: Cystic fibrosis is a congenital (autosomal-recessive) disorder of the exocrine glands, including the salivary glands. The CFTR gene defect causes abnormally thick, viscous secretions; in the airways this impairs mucociliary clearance, leading to colonisation by pathogens and a markedly increased incidence of acute respiratory infections.

378835.long_answer: BRCA1 (Breast Cancer 1) is a tumor-suppressor gene whose pathogenic variants are classically linked to hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndromes, and, to a lesser extent, increased risks for other malignancies (e.g., prostate, pancreatic). BRCA1 is not part of the spectrum of genes known to cause disorders of keratinization such as palmoplantar keratoderma. Palmoplantar keratoderma is typically associated with mutations in genes encoding structural skin proteins (e.g., KRT1, KRT9, KRT6C, DSG1, LOR), enzymes such as cathepsin C (CTSC), or transcription factors like TP63, among others. No peer-reviewed studies, clinical genetics databases (OMIM, ClinVar, HGMD), or dermatology textbooks report an etiologic or mechanistic link between BRCA1 variants and palmoplantar keratoderma. Therefore, the statement that BRCA1 is associated with palmoplantar keratoderma is not supported by established biomedical evidence.

629757.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the MAGI2 gene are a recognized cause of Infantile Epileptic Spasms Syndrome (IESS-7).  Independent reports have also shown that heterozygous loss-of-function or disruptive copy-number changes in MAGI2 lead to congenital hyperinsulinism, producing recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia.  Thus, the same gene that underlies infantile spasms can additionally manifest with hypoglycemia.

356307.long_answer: Bejel is caused by Treponema pallidum subsp. endemicum. The infection elicits circulating antibodies that are reliably detected with the same treponemal and non-treponemal serologic tests used for syphilis (e.g., FTA-ABS, TPPA, VDRL/RPR). Therefore, performing serologic testing allows identification of the antibodies produced against the pathogen and is the standard diagnostic method for bejel.

146151.long_answer: In Neurofibromatosis type I, Unidentified Bright Objects (UBOs) appear as T2-hyperintense foci on MRI. They most frequently localize to the basal ganglia—particularly the globus pallidus and putamen—reflecting focal myelin vacuolization in this deep gray-matter region.

461165.long_answer: During an active flare-up of fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva, new ectopic bone is laid down. This increased osteogenic activity commonly leads to a transient rise in the bone-derived enzyme alkaline phosphatase in the patient’s serum; therefore, elevated serum alkaline phosphatase is often used as a biochemical indicator that a flare-up is occurring.

137501.long_answer: In severe drug-induced skin reactions such as Stevens–Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis, therapeutic plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) is sometimes employed. The procedure removes circulating drug metabolites, immune complexes, and pro-inflammatory cytokines from the patient’s plasma, helping to halt epidermal destruction and improve outcomes when the reaction is life-threatening.

330935.long_answer: The American Cancer Society (ACS) does not endorse therapeutic touch as an effective treatment for multiple chemical sensitivity (or for any other specific medical condition). In its reviews of complementary and alternative therapies, the ACS states that scientific evidence is lacking to show that therapeutic touch can prevent or cure disease, reduce symptoms, or improve health outcomes beyond a placebo effect. The organization emphasizes that well-controlled studies have not demonstrated objective benefits of therapeutic touch, and it advises patients to rely on proven, evidence-based treatments. Therefore, the claim that the ACS supports therapeutic touch for treating multiple chemical sensitivity is not consistent with the ACS’s published position.

260702.long_answer: Brain-lung-thyroid syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the NKX2-1 (TTF-1) transcription factor. The disorder presents at birth with primary congenital hypothyroidism from thyroid dysgenesis, together with neonatal respiratory distress or chronic lung disease and variable neurological abnormalities. Impaired brain growth is frequent, so affected infants and children may develop microcephaly in addition to motor delay and chorea. Thus this single congenital syndrome links primary hypothyroidism with the potential for microcephaly.

443279.long_answer: Concrescence is a developmental dental anomaly in which two adjacent teeth become united solely by their cementum layers; the enamel and dentin remain separate. This fusion limited to cementum distinguishes concrescence from true tooth fusion, where dentin is also joined.

116836.long_answer: Rüdiger syndrome follows an autosomal-recessive pattern of inheritance; the causative mutations lie on one of the non-sex (autosomal) chromosomes, so the trait is transmitted independently of the sex chromosomes and affects males and females equally when both copies of the autosomal gene are defective.

169264.long_answer: Distal arthrogryposis is most commonly caused by autosomal-dominant missense mutations in the MYH3 gene, which encodes the embryonic skeletal-muscle myosin heavy chain. Altered myosin impairs fetal muscle contractility, leading to the characteristic distal joint contractures seen in this condition.

346532.long_answer: If low-dose levodopa does not fully control the dystonia in autosomal dominant GTP-cyclohydrolase I deficiency, dopamine agonists can be added. The agents most often recommended as this second-line option are the ergot-derived dopamine agonists pergolide and bromocriptine, which directly stimulate striatal D2/D1 receptors and can enhance dopaminergic tone when levodopa alone is insufficient or poorly tolerated.

382331.long_answer: In Glycogen Storage Disease type I, the cornerstone for preventing hypoglycemia is the scheduled ingestion of uncooked cornstarch, whose slow digestion supplies a steady stream of glucose. One level tablespoon of dry uncooked cornstarch (≈15 g) contains about 14 g of carbohydrate, providing roughly 55–60 kilocalories.

928317.long_answer: Oral lutein supplementation is thought to help slow cone degeneration in hereditary cone or cone-rod dystrophies. Lutein is a macular carotenoid that concentrates in the fovea, where it scavenges reactive oxygen species and absorbs blue light, thereby protecting cone photoreceptors. Small clinical studies have shown that daily lutein increases macular pigment optical density and is associated with a slower decline in cone-mediated visual function, supporting its use to delay progression of cone dystrophy.

767768.long_answer: When an arachnoid cyst produces neurological symptoms, one accepted therapeutic option is surgical cyst fenestration—either microsurgical or endoscopic. Opening (fenestrating) the cyst wall allows its cerebrospinal fluid to communicate with normal CSF spaces, relieving mass effect and lowering intracystic pressure, which typically improves or resolves symptoms.

630367.long_answer: Hyperreflexia is a classic upper-motor-neuron sign that follows damage to descending inhibitory pathways in the spinal cord. Evaluation and management of spinal cord injuries and their neurological sequelae, including exaggerated reflexes, fall under the domain of neurology, the medical specialty focused on disorders of the central and peripheral nervous system.

375903.long_answer: Although ainhum was originally recognised in West Africa, the first report of the condition from the Western hemisphere came from the then-British colony of British Guiana (present-day Guyana), making it the earliest British colonial site in the West to document the disease.

461848.long_answer: De novo gain-of-function mutations in the KCNT1 gene, which encodes the sodium-activated potassium channel KNa1.1, are the most common genetic cause of malignant migrating partial seizures of infancy (MMPSI). Patients with KCNT1-related MMPSI often develop progressive cerebral and cerebellar atrophy on neuroimaging, leading to enlarged ventricles and widened subarachnoid spaces—i.e., marked changes in the cerebrospinal fluid spaces.

378961.long_answer: Chronic mountain sickness (Monge’s disease) causes sustained hypoxemia that drives excessive erythrocytosis and marked pulmonary vasoconstriction. The resulting pulmonary hypertension places an increasing pressure load on the right ventricle; if the process is not corrected, right-ventricular hypertrophy and dilation ensue, culminating in cor pulmonale (right-sided heart failure). Thus, untreated chronic mountain sickness can progress to cor pulmonale.

194432.long_answer: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis is an opportunistic infection that occurs almost exclusively in people with severely compromised immune systems, such as those with advanced HIV/AIDS or after organ transplantation. The disease primarily affects the retina, producing visual disturbances (floaters, blurry vision, scotomata) rather than systemic illness. Although low-grade fever can occasionally be reported, it is an uncommon finding; most patients have no fever or other systemic symptoms, making fever a rare presentation in CMV retinitis.

868294.long_answer: New protein-coding genes can arise directly from previously non-coding DNA through de novo gene birth (also called de novo gene origination). During this process, random mutations create an open reading frame in a non-coding region, followed by acquisition of regulatory elements that allow transcription and translation. Natural selection can then fix functional variants, yielding a novel gene that, in some cases—such as loci implicated in Noonan syndrome—may influence disease phenotypes.

253991.long_answer: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is a chromosomal disorder in which newborns typically show generalized hypotonia, resulting in weak or absent primitive neonatal reflexes such as the Moro and grasp reflexes. At birth they also display characteristic dysmorphic facial features—flat facial profile, up-slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, small ears, and a flat nasal bridge. The combination of absent neonatal reflexes and abnormal facial appearance is therefore classically associated with Down syndrome.

792044.long_answer: German Emperor Kaiser Wilhelm II (1859-1941) suffered a traction injury to the brachial plexus during a difficult breech delivery, damaging the upper roots (C5–C6) and producing the characteristic arm weakness and contracture of Erb’s palsy that he displayed throughout his life.

710389.long_answer: In Noonan syndrome, developmental anomalies of the mid-gut can occur, most notably intestinal malrotation. When the intestines fail to rotate and fix properly during embryogenesis, narrow mesenteric attachments leave the mid-gut prone to twisting around the superior mesenteric vessels, producing a mid-gut (intestinal) volvulus. Thus, intestinal malrotation is the congenital anomaly linked to Noonan syndrome that can precipitate volvulus.

484034.long_answer: Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany was born in 1859 with a traumatic obstetric injury to the upper brachial plexus (C5–C6 roots), producing Erb-Duchenne palsy. The resulting paralysis and contracture left his left arm shortened and weakened, a well-documented disability throughout his life.

177775.long_answer: The condition carries the name of its discoverer, the Norwegian physician Ole Lyngstadaas, who first described the autosomal-recessive cholestatic liver disease that is now referred to as Lyngstadaas syndrome.

907918.long_answer: Cri du chat syndrome, caused by a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-), presents with marked intellectual disability, a characteristic dysmorphic facial appearance (hypertelorism, epicanthal folds, micrognathia, round face) and is classically accompanied by microcephaly. These features make it the well-recognized genetic disorder linking distinctive facies, cognitive impairment and microcephaly.

391971.long_answer: Environmental or internal cues repeatedly paired with alcohol’s rewarding pharmacological effects become conditioned stimuli through classical (Pavlovian) conditioning. These conditioned stimuli later evoke craving and drinking automatically, thus perpetuating and maintaining alcohol dependence even in the absence of the original reinforcing effects.

243719.long_answer: Ergophobia (an excessive fear of work or the workplace) is typically classified as a situational or performance-related manifestation of social anxiety disorder (social phobia). Large epidemiologic studies and meta-analyses show that people with social anxiety disorder have significantly higher rates of suicidal ideation and suicide attempts than the general population, giving this disorder a recognized high risk of suicide.

147846.long_answer: Confirmation of Glycogen Storage Disease type I is obtained by performing a liver biopsy and directly measuring glucose-6-phosphatase activity in the tissue; absent or markedly reduced enzymatic activity establishes the diagnosis.

506742.long_answer: In distal (type I) renal tubular acidosis, the persistently alkaline urine promotes calcium-phosphate stone formation and nephrocalcinosis. The resulting stones or crystal deposits often irritate the urinary tract, leading to microscopic or gross blood in the urine. Therefore, hematuria—defined as the presence of blood in the urine—is a common clinical symptom associated with distal renal tubular acidosis.

218229.long_answer: X-linked myopathy with excessive autophagy is a rare inherited neuromuscular disorder that presents with progressive muscle weakness. The evaluation and diagnosis of such primary muscle diseases—including clinical examination, electromyography, muscle biopsy interpretation, and ordering of confirmatory genetic testing—are typically performed by neurologists, especially those with neuromuscular subspecialty training. Therefore, the medical specialty most likely to establish the diagnosis is Neurology.

713115.long_answer: An elliptical trainer (also called a cross-trainer) guides the feet through an oval, or elliptical, path that merges the vertical stepping motion of a stair-climber with the horizontal stride of walking or running on a treadmill. This hybrid movement allows users to obtain the cardiovascular benefits of both exercises while minimizing joint impact.

373472.long_answer:
Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a neurocutaneous (phakomatosis) disorder produced by pathogenic variants in TSC1 or TSC2.  Skin findings are among the most consistent diagnostic features.  Two of the best-known cutaneous manifestations are:

1. Facial angiofibromas (formerly called adenoma sebaceum) – multiple red-to-flesh-coloured papules clustered on the nose and malar areas of the cheeks.
2. Fibrous facial/cephalic plaques and other connective-tissue hamartomas that often look and feel like thickened, scar-like skin.  When these occur on the face they are frequently described clinically as "facial scarring" or "scar-like plaques."  In addition, the papules of angiofibromas themselves may coalesce or be treated and leave pitted or fibrous scars.

Because patients with TSC characteristically exhibit both angiofibromas and scar-like fibrous facial lesions, the disorder is indeed associated with facial scarring and angiofibromas according to established medical literature and diagnostic criteria.

196750.long_answer: In the ILAE 2022 classification of the epilepsies, Dravet syndrome is listed under the group of “developmental and epileptic encephalopathies” (DEE). These syndromes are characterized by early-onset, treatment-resistant seizures accompanied by developmental slowing or regression that is partly driven by the epileptic activity itself. Dravet syndrome, typically linked to pathogenic SCN1A variants, fits this definition and is explicitly named as a prototypical DEE in the 2022 ILAE framework.

662698.long_answer: Spondylocostal dysostosis (Jarcho-Levin syndrome) causes multiple segmentation defects of the vertebrae and ribs. Prenatal ultrasound often shows ribs of unequal length and irregular spacing that can mimic the multiple rib fractures seen in lethal osteogenesis imperfecta type II, leading to possible misdiagnosis. Recognizing the asymmetric, congenital pattern of rib malformations—rather than true fractures—helps differentiate spondylocostal dysostosis from osteogenesis imperfecta.

462127.long_answer: Doxycycline, a long-acting member of the tetracycline class, is given as 200 mg orally once weekly and has been shown in controlled trials to prevent leptospiral infection in people exposed to contaminated water or soil. Beyond its medical role, doxycycline is frequently embedded in or blended with molten polycarbonate during moulding of medical-grade plastic devices; the antibiotic remains in the polymer matrix and is slowly released, giving the finished polycarbonate material intrinsic antimicrobial properties.

563835.long_answer: Anteroposterior and lateral plain X-ray films of the cervical spine and shoulder girdle show the elevated, medially rotated scapula (and any omovertebral bone), thereby confirming Sprengel’s deformity.

278778.long_answer: Epidemiologic studies of post-9/11 service members show that soldiers in the U.S. Army, the branch most frequently deployed in prolonged ground-combat operations, exhibit the highest rates of post-traumatic stress disorder compared with other branches (e.g., Navy, Air Force). Intensive, repeated combat exposure among Army personnel is the primary driver of this elevated PTSD prevalence.

903208.long_answer: Da Costa’s (effort) syndrome was studied and described in First-World-War soldiers by the British physician Arthur Cecil Alport. The same clinician later (1927) reported a familial form of progressive hereditary nephritis with deafness, which has since been named Alport syndrome. Thus, the genetic disorder associated with the physician who described Da Costa’s syndrome is Alport syndrome.

837627.long_answer: The PAX2 gene encodes a transcription factor that is essential for normal ureteric-bud outgrowth and branching during kidney development. Abnormal expression or mutation of PAX2 disrupts the signalling between the ureteric bud and the metanephric mesenchyme, leading to renal dysplasia with cyst formation. Elevated or altered PAX2 activity has been repeatedly documented in human multicystic dysplastic kidney specimens, and inherited PAX2 mutations produce syndromes (e.g., renal-coloboma) in which multicystic dysplastic kidneys are a characteristic finding. Hence PAX2 is the gene most commonly implicated in the pathogenesis of multicystic dysplastic kidney.

797994.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in TGM5, the gene that encodes epidermal transglutaminase-5, cause acral/peeling skin syndrome. Affected individuals typically show lifelong superficial peeling of the stratum corneum, especially on hands and feet, and many patients also exhibit palmoplantar hyperhidrosis. Thus TGM5 is the gene linked to both peeling skin syndrome and excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis).

343889.long_answer: Saal-Bulas syndrome (a SALL4-related Duane–radial-ray disorder) commonly includes congenital conductive or sensorineural hearing loss. The standard management of this particular symptom is early audiologic assessment and fitting of hearing aids, which restore auditory input, support speech-language development, and improve quality of life.

866603.long_answer: Erysipelas often presents with abrupt high fever accompanied by chills— involuntary shivering episodes that raise body temperature. Chills are the same physiological response the body mounts when exposed to cold or during extreme fear, mediated by hypothalamic thermoregulatory centers and sympathetic activation.

622016.long_answer: Paramyotonia congenita is a sodium-channel myopathy in which attacks are precipitated by cold, exercise, or an acute rise in serum potassium. Eating potassium-rich foods, classically bananas, can raise serum K⁺ and thereby trigger the characteristic stiffness and weakness in affected individuals.

459042.long_answer: IgG antibodies directed against hepatitis B surface antigen (anti-HBs) are actively transported across the placenta via Fc receptors. These maternal IgG molecules coat and neutralise any hepatitis B virions that may reach the intervillous space, so the fetus is passively protected and in-utero transmission is largely prevented; most neonatal infection therefore occurs during labour and delivery rather than across the intact placenta.

961968.long_answer: In the autosomal-dominant pure form of hereditary spastic paraplegia, weakness is most prominent in ankle dorsiflexion; the tibialis anterior muscle, the principal dorsiflexor of the foot, is characteristically weak, leading to early foot-drop despite otherwise predominant spasticity of the lower limbs.

773757.long_answer: In published case series of females with tetrasomy X (48,XXXX), congenital heart disease is relatively common; the lesion reported most often is persistence of the fetal ductus arteriosus. Patent ductus arteriosus has been documented more frequently than other defects such as atrial or ventricular septal defects, making it the heart defect most commonly associated with tetrasomy X.

271494.long_answer: Dr. Janey Wiggs’ group showed that loss-of-function mutations in the TEK gene (also called TIE2), which encodes an endothelial receptor tyrosine kinase essential for Schlemm’s canal formation, cause primary congenital glaucoma by impairing aqueous humor outflow and raising intra-ocular pressure.

170539.long_answer: When dysphagia is not managed, patients often cannot take in enough food or fluids, leading to protein-energy and micronutrient deficits—i.e., malnutrition. Chronic or severe gastritis can likewise reduce appetite, cause vomiting, impair nutrient absorption, and produce chronic blood loss, all of which are well-documented pathways to the same condition. Thus malnutrition is both a consequence of untreated dysphagia and a recognized complication of gastritis.

961046.long_answer: A trichofolliculoma on the eyelid is an eyelid skin adnexal lesion whose excision and reconstruction must preserve eyelid margin integrity and ocular surface protection. These procedures fall within the subspecialty of oculoplastic (ophthalmic plastic and reconstructive) surgery, a branch of ophthalmology trained to manage benign and malignant eyelid tumors safely while maintaining eyelid function and cosmesis.

142344.long_answer: In Filippi syndrome the cutaneous syndactyly of the fingers frequently extends to the deeper structures; the lumbrical muscle can span the fused digits and limit independent movement. Corrective hand surgery therefore often includes division or excision of this aberrant lumbrical muscle to allow proper separation and function of the affected fingers.

273247.long_answer: Leukemias, including the minimally differentiated (M0) subtype of acute myeloblastic (myeloid) leukemia, are managed by hematologists (often trained as hematologist-oncologists). This specialty focuses on disorders of the blood and bone marrow and directs diagnostic evaluation, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and stem-cell transplantation for AML patients.

272081.long_answer: In patients with schizophrenia who develop psychogenic polydipsia, dilutional hyponatremia commonly accompanies the excessive water intake. The large volumes of free water ingested overwhelm renal excretory capacity, lowering serum sodium and leading to water-intoxication episodes; therefore, hyponatremia is considered a frequent comorbid condition with psychogenic polydipsia in this population.

910463.long_answer: Biemond syndrome (also called the coloboma–brachydactyly syndrome) is classically associated with brachydactyly that involves the terminal, or distal, phalanges of the fingers and toes. These end-bones are shortened or absent, whereas the more proximal hand and foot bones are usually normal.

717340.long_answer: The visual problems in Cohen syndrome arise from a progressive pigmentary retinopathy—degeneration of the retinal tissue, which is an outgrowth of the brain. Damage to the retina leads to high myopia, night blindness, and progressive loss of visual acuity seen in affected individuals.

247532.long_answer: Escherichia coli grows best, and is able to initiate infection, in a neutral-to-slightly alkaline milieu. The peritoneal cavity is normally close to physiologic pH (about 7.35–7.45). If E. coli escapes the intestine into this environment, the neutral pH (~7.4) permits rapid bacterial multiplication and the release of endotoxin, leading to acute bacterial peritonitis. In more acidic conditions (pH < 6), its growth is markedly suppressed, but at the physiologic pH of ~7.4 it can readily cause peritoneal infection.

659629.long_answer: Hypersensitivity to wheat gluten, as in coeliac (gluten-sensitive) disease, is well documented to cause a seronegative spondyloarthropathy termed enteropathic arthritis. This arthritis is regarded as an extra-intestinal manifestation of gluten/wheat sensitivity and typically involves large peripheral joints and sometimes the sacro-iliac joints.

470500.long_answer: Corneal-cerebellar syndrome combines bilateral fleck-type corneal dystrophy with progressive cerebellar ataxia. Families with this phenotype have been shown to carry heterozygous missense mutations in the PIKFYVE gene, which encodes phosphoinositide kinase FYVE-type zinc finger–containing enzyme. These mutations disrupt phosphoinositide metabolism in both corneal keratocytes and cerebellar neurons, accounting for the characteristic corneal dystrophy and neurologic involvement seen in the syndrome.

566529.long_answer: A short Type IV laryngeal cleft reaches from the larynx into the upper (cervical) segment of the trachea. Surgical repair is done through a lateral cervical (neck) approach that exposes and closes the cleft in the posterior wall of the cervical trachea.

147774.long_answer: The Martinican pit viper, now classified as Bothrops lanceolatus, was first formally described in 1790 by the French zoologist Pierre Joseph Bonnaterre, whose name is cited as the taxonomic authority for the species.

317816.long_answer: The nephropathy in multicentric carpotarsal osteolysis syndrome is a non-immune, MAFB-related focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Multiple case reports show that corticosteroids, cyclosporine and other immunosuppressive agents do not halt proteinuria or prevent progression to renal failure, indicating that immunosuppressive drugs are ineffective for this renal complication.

734563.long_answer: Genome‐wide association studies have consistently identified variants in the IRF6 gene (Interferon Regulatory Factor 6) as strongly associated with cleft lip and/or palate. IRF6 mutations underlie Van der Woude syndrome, the most common syndromic form of craniofacial clefting, and common non-coding variants at the IRF6 locus are a major genetic risk factor for nonsyndromic cleft lip with or without cleft palate.

504872.long_answer: The cutaneous reaction of livedoid dermatitis (Nicolau syndrome) after drug injections is produced by acute ischemia of the skin and subcutaneous tissues, caused by arterial spasm or thrombotic occlusion at the injection site. This ischemia deprives cells of oxygen, leading to the characteristic ischemic (hypoxic) necrosis that underlies the lesion.

336490.long_answer: A missense or duplicative mutation in the amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene, located on chromosome 21, is a well-established cause of autosomal-dominant early-onset Alzheimer’s disease. The altered APP undergoes aberrant β- and γ-secretase cleavage, generating excess Aβ42 peptides that aggregate into extracellular amyloid plaques. These amyloid deposits trigger tau hyper-phosphorylation inside neurons, resulting in the intracellular neurofibrillary tangles that are pathognomonic of Alzheimer’s disease.

930570.long_answer: Fusobacterium nucleatum, an oral anaerobic Gram-negative bacterium, is consistently enriched in colorectal cancer tissue and stool. Its abundance rises from normal mucosa to adenomas and carcinomas, and it promotes tumorigenesis through factors such as the FadA adhesin and immune modulation. Quantitative detection of F. nucleatum DNA in fecal samples accurately discriminates patients with advanced adenomas or early colorectal cancer, making it a useful biomarker for early prediction of high-risk bowel lesions.

526143.long_answer: Activated charcoal is routinely administered in cases of barbiturate overdose because it adsorbs the drug in the gastrointestinal tract and limits systemic absorption. The same gastrointestinal decontamination approach is widely employed for many other acute drug overdoses (e.g., tricyclic antidepressants, acetaminophen), making activated charcoal a common, broad-spectrum initial treatment.

224266.long_answer: If a woman acquires primary Toxoplasma gondii infection during pregnancy, the parasite can cross the placenta and infect the fetus, leading to congenital toxoplasmosis. This can result in miscarriage, stillbirth, or severe neonatal complications such as hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, and intracranial calcifications.

413157.long_answer: Neuropathological studies of Unverricht–Lundborg disease (EPM1) brains show an up-regulation of the γ-aminobutyric acid type A (GABAA) receptor. The density of these inhibitory neurotransmitter receptors is significantly higher than in unaffected brains, a finding that correlates with the clinical responsiveness of patients to benzodiazepines, which act by potentiating GABAA receptor–mediated inhibition.

248337.long_answer: In infants with tricuspid atresia, a systemic-to-pulmonary arterial shunt such as the Blalock-Taussig shunt is commonly created to augment pulmonary blood flow. By connecting the subclavian (or innominate) artery to the pulmonary artery, this palliative procedure directs oxygen-poor systemic blood into the lungs, improving oxygenation until later definitive surgeries (e.g., Glenn or Fontan) can be performed.

772677.long_answer: In the novel, mission director Eva Stratt has Ryland Grace injected with ketamine, a dissociative anesthetic that produces profound sedation and both retrograde and anterograde amnesia. The drug’s well-known ability to erase recent memories and render a patient unconscious ensured Grace would not recall being forced onto the Hail Mary spacecraft.

285468.long_answer: Beyond progressive lower-limb spasticity, many individuals with hereditary spastic paraplegia report paresthesia—abnormal skin sensations such as tingling, prickling, or ‘pins-and-needles.’ These sensory disturbances reflect involvement of long sensory tracts alongside corticospinal tract degeneration characteristic of the disorder.

444492.long_answer: Nager syndrome (acrofacial dysostosis, Nager type) is most often produced by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the SF3B4 gene on chromosome 1. Because the defective allele resides on an autosome and a single copy is sufficient to cause the condition, the disorder follows an autosomal dominant Mendelian inheritance pattern.

866223.long_answer: Familial benign copper deficiency results from mutations in the ATP7A copper-transport gene located on the X chromosome. Because the mutant allele is carried on the X chromosome and disease manifests primarily in hemizygous males while heterozygous females are usually asymptomatic carriers, the condition follows an X-linked recessive mode of inheritance.

697339.long_answer: Glycine encephalopathy (non-ketotic hyperglycinemia) is caused by defects in the mitochondrial glycine cleavage system. Because this multi-enzyme complex resides on the inner mitochondrial membrane, mitochondrial dysfunction in glycine degradation leads to systemic accumulation of glycine and the characteristic neurological symptoms.

777713.long_answer: In minimally differentiated (M0) acute myeloblastic leukemia, cytochemical stains for myeloperoxidase are usually negative, so lineage must be confirmed molecularly. This is done by amplifying and detecting sequences of the myeloperoxidase (MPO) gene with the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), demonstrating the presence of MPO despite absent enzyme activity.

333041.long_answer: In the early-20th-century United States, the most notorious pellagra epidemics were concentrated in the impoverished mill towns and farm communities of the Pee Dee River basin in South and North Carolina. Public-health investigators, including Joseph Goldberger, documented thousands of cases along this river, and the region became emblematic of the U.S. pellagra outbreak linked to monotonous corn-based diets deficient in niacin.

665287.long_answer: Spasticity in Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts (MLC) is managed symptomatically, and the antispastic agent most frequently prescribed is baclofen. Baclofen, a GABA-B receptor agonist, reduces excitatory neurotransmitter release in the spinal cord and thereby diminishes muscle hypertonia, making it the standard first-line pharmacologic therapy for spasticity in MLC and other leukodystrophies.

894323.long_answer: Among people who carry the same causal genetic alteration for Müllerian agenesis (MRKH syndrome), the trait does not manifest to the same degree in every individual. This phenomenon, known as variable expressivity, means that identical or similar mutations can produce a spectrum of clinical features—from complete absence of the uterus and upper vagina to milder malformations—thereby explaining the differing severity of symptoms observed in affected individuals.

254127.long_answer: Carney-Stratakis syndrome (the ʻdyadʼ) is defined by the coexistence of gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GISTs) with catecholamine-secreting paragangliomas. These tumours arise from the neuroendocrine paraganglia (chromaffin tissue related to the adrenal medulla) and may function like pheochromocytomas by producing catecholamines; thus the hormone-producing glandular element involved is the paraganglionic system.

509106.long_answer: Movement disorders such as dystonia and choreoathetosis that develop after kernicterus are often treated with benzodiazepines (e.g., clonazepam or diazepam). These drugs enhance GABA-mediated inhibition within the basal ganglia and other motor pathways, helping to dampen the hyperkinetic movements produced by bilirubin-induced neuronal injury.

903302.long_answer: Molybdenum is an essential cofactor for xanthine oxidase, the enzyme that converts xanthine to uric acid. When dietary molybdenum is insufficient, xanthine oxidase activity falls, xanthine accumulates, and poorly soluble xanthine precipitates in the renal tract, leading to kidney (xanthine) stones.

449497.long_answer: Autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia type II corresponds to spinocerebellar ataxia 7, which is caused by CAG-repeat expansion in the ATXN7 gene (ataxin-7). Ataxin-7 is an integral subunit of the SAGA (Spt–Ada–GCN5 acetyltransferase) transcription co-activator complex, and its transcription is regulated through the chromatin-remodeling and histone-acetylation activities of SAGA. Hence, ATXN7 is the gene whose expression is controlled by the SAGA complex.

372869.long_answer: Yes. In the United States, the National Institutes of Health (NIH)—specifically its Office of Rare Diseases Research (ORDR) within the National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences (NCATS)—maintains the Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center (GARD). GARD includes an entry for “Fetal trimethadione syndrome” (also called “trimethadione embryopathy”) and designates it as a rare disease, i.e., affecting fewer than 200,000 people in the U.S. Therefore, at least one government agency (the NIH) officially classifies fetal trimethadione syndrome as a rare disease.

866643.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the COL4A1 gene (encoding the α1-chain of type IV collagen) are a well-documented cause of hereditary cerebral small-vessel disease that often presents prenatally as intracerebral haemorrhage and porencephaly. Several families and case reports have also shown that children with COL4A1 mutations display the characteristic facial gestalt and neuro-behavioural profile used to diagnose fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, leading to recognition of COL4A1 mutation as a genetic mimic and risk factor for FASD as well as a proven cause of porencephaly.

605258.long_answer: Several New York City firefighters who inhaled the caustic, silica- and metal-laden dust cloud on 9/11 subsequently developed sarcoidosis—a multisystem granulomatous disease characterized by non-caseating granulomas, most often in the lungs and lymph nodes. Epidemiologic studies of FDNY personnel showed a markedly increased incidence of new-onset sarcoidosis after World Trade Center dust exposure, linking the inhaled particulate matter to the firefighter’s disease.

568735.long_answer: Onycholysis is the distal separation of the nail plate from the nail bed. When a thorough evaluation fails to reveal any local trauma, dermatologic disorder, systemic illness, infection, or drug exposure responsible for the detachment, the condition is classified as idiopathic (or primary) onycholysis, meaning the cause is unknown.
